title: Search insert position
prompt:
PageTurn's catalog is sorted by reading level. When a student is assessed at level target, the app needs the index of the first book at that level or above: the target's index if it exists, otherwise the index where it would be inserted to keep the list sorted.

Write searchInsert(nums, target). If the target appears more than once, return its first index. Must run in O(log n) time.

Examples with nums = [1, 3, 5, 6]:

  • searchInsert(nums, 5) → 2 (found)
  • searchInsert(nums, 2) → 1 (would go between 1 and 3)
  • searchInsert(nums, 7) → 4 (after everything)
  • searchInsert(nums, 0) → 0

Constraints: 0 ≤ nums.length ≤ 105, sorted in non-decreasing order, values can be negative.

tests.name: target missing: insert position in the middle
matches a linear scan on many small inputs

hints: Sorted array + find a position + O(log n) = binary search. Phrase it as a yes/no question that flips once: "is nums[i] >= target?" The answer is the first yes.
Use lo = 0, hi = nums.length (one past the end, so "insert at the end" works). While lo < hi: if nums[mid] >= target, the first yes is at mid or before, so hi = mid; otherwise lo = mid + 1.

Shape:

let lo = 0, hi = nums.length;
while (lo < hi) {
  const mid = lo + Math.floor((hi - lo) / 2);
  if (nums[mid] >= target) hi = mid;
  else lo = mid + 1;
}
return lo;
explain:
Time O(log n), space O(1). Each step halves the range: 100,000 books take about 17 checks instead of up to 100,000.

This exact function is called lower bound (C++ std::lower_bound, Python bisect_left). Databases do the same thing inside each B-tree page to find which child to follow.

In an interview: "The array is sorted, so I'll binary search for the first index where the value is at least the target. I keep the invariant that everything before lo is smaller and everything from hi on is at least the target, so when lo meets hi that's the answer. O(log n) time, O(1) space."
